English as a global language
The text below was published in the Financial Times in 2018.
Discuss what you feel are the most important issues raised here relating to the changing
use of English as a global language. You should refer to specific details from the text as well as
to ideas and examples from your wider study.
The PewDiePie effect: how a new global generation learnt perfect English
The world’s most popular YouTuber is probably PewDiePie. He lives in England, but he
is a Swede called Felix Kjellberg. Born in 1989, he represents the first global generation
in which tens of millions of people from outside the English-speaking world speak perfect
English. That shift is ominous for the US and UK. Thanks to English, these countries 5
have dominated the global conversation. Their entertainment, media, university and tech
sectors bestraddle the world. But now the PewDiePie generation, machine translation,
and the political climate are combining to threaten their dominance.
A few non-native speakers have always managed to sneak into the global English
conversation. In music, for instance, think of PewDiePie’s fellow Nordics Abba and Björk. 10
But most ambitious foreigners were held back because they spoke not English, but
Globish: a simple, dull, idiom-free, cripplingly accented version of English with a small
vocabulary. So they rarely sounded as fun, clever or cool in English as native speakers.
This had fateful consequences. “What is well articulated in English on the internet
becomes ‘truth,’” says Japanese writer Minae Mizumura in The Fall of Language in the 15
Age of English. Perfect English is not only heard more, but also taken more seriously
than what’s said in other languages, she argues.
And the production line of perfect English-speakers hums ever faster. More and more
universities around the world offer courses in English. The Netherlands sets the pace in
Europe, followed by the Scandinavians. These countries are now attracting world-class 20
foreign academics, and that’s before the anticipated post-Brexit exodus from British
universities, from which continental Europe should benefit. Amsterdam and Copenhagen
are already effectively bilingual. Berlin and Paris aren’t far behind.
Next, the US and UK will lose their dominance of media. Machine translation improves
by the week. In a couple of years, a top-class newspaper like Die Zeit will produce its 25
German edition, then press “translate” and get a very decent English version in an
instant.
Everyone now piously preaches multilingualism, but it’s not going to happen. About 1.5
billion people are learning English. And the more people who speak English, the more
useful English becomes. Anyway, the PewDiePie generation won’t let you learn their 30
own languages. Try going to Sweden and speaking bad Swedish. You’ll be forced into
English in seconds.
The next global ruling class will perceive the world chiefly in English. That will be a loss.
As Mizumura says, you can only see what your language allows you to express. But
when perfect English becomes standard, Brits and Americans lose their advantage. 35
Notes:
post-Brexit: after the United Kingdom leaves the European Union
